Benchmarking CometBFT with Asymmetric Grid Quorum
Systems
Michael Senn
michael.senn@unibe.ch
University of Bern
Institute of Computer Science
Bern, Switzerland

christian.cachin@unibe.ch

A Artifact Appendix
A.1 Abstract
This artifact accompanies a paper 1 introducingasymmetric grid
quorum systems, a quorum system construction which is based on
differences of real-world processes such as their operating system,
or physical location.
The artifact implements a benchmark comparing two versions of
CometBFT, a widely-used state-machine replication software. One
version, titledbaseline, is an unmodified recent stable version of
CometBFT. The other, titledgrid, is a version of CometBFT modified
to work with these grid quorums instead.
The artifact consists of a pipeline to assist with deploying CometBFT
on a set of machines, a benchmarking client to apply a workload
and collect performance data, and a data analysis and visualization
toolchain to prepare figures based on this data. Results show that
adding support for these quorum systems can be done with rela-
tively low effort, and that doing so has no adverse effect on the
performance of a real-world system such as CometBFT.
The artifact is provided as a set of public Github repositories, as
well as as a point-in-time snapshot on Zenodo. All code is licensed
under an Apache 2.0 license.
A.2 Description & Requirements
For organizational reasons, our artifact is split into multiple com-
ponents. These are:
tenderload Main benchmarking pipeline, containing code
to automatically provision machines, run the benchmark,
collect data, and analyze results. Also contains the raw data
used to produce the results of the paper.
tendergrid A fork of CometBFT, with added support for asym-
metric quorum systems.
tendercounter A replicated application running on top of
CometBFT.
asymmetric-quorums A Go library providing methods to
interface with asymmetric quorum systems.
Each component contains aREADME.md explaining how to use the
tools contained within. To get started with the artifact as a whole,
we recommend consulting the top-level readme of the tenderload
repository. It contains thorough step-by-step instructions on how
to reproduce the results of the paper.
A.2.1 Security, privacy, and ethical concerns.There is no direct risk
with executing any of the artifacts, other than the risk inherent
1https://doi.org/10.1145/3830454.3832646
with running software. None of the artifact contains functionality
purposefully made to be harmful or destructive.
A.2.2 How to access.We provide the artifact as a set of public
repositories on GitHub2345 as well as a point-in-time snapshot on
Zenodo6.
Most of these repositories are labelled with a git tagccs26, mark-
ing the version used to produce the paper’s results. The tender-
grid repository instead contains two tags, ccs26-baseline and
ccs26-grid, marking the version of CometBFT used for baseline
measurements, and those with support for asymmetric grid quo-
rums respectively. The snapshot on Zenodo instead contains a
single zip archive for each repository and tag.
A.2.3 Hardware dependencies.To make use of the full artifact, a set
of machines on which to host a CometBFT deployment is required.
These can be hosted in a cloud, on a local hypervisor, or even as a
set of VMs on a personal computer. To reproduce the results of the
paper fully, you must be able to host 49 VMs, each with 4 CPU cores
and 4 GiB of RAM, connected by a high-speed network, without
causing resource contention among the machines. The machines
themselves do not require specific hardware, but should be based
on the x86 architecture to make use of pre-compiled binaries. Other
architectures will work as well, but may require building parts of
the artifact for that architecture, first.
A.2.4 Software dependencies.Depending on the parts of the ar-
tifact one wants to use, different software is required. Detailed
instructions are provided in the main readme of the tenderload
repository. Broadly speaking, these are:
•Debian 12, as operating system of the benchmark VMs.
•Ansible, to make use of the deployment pipeline
• Docker, to run the distributed application on the bench-
marking machines and, optionally, build containers. We
provide pre-built containers for x86.
• Optionally Go, to build the benchmarking client. We pro-
vide a pre-built binary for x86.
• Python, to make use of the data-analysis and visualization
pipeline.
A.2.5 Benchmarks.No specific datasets are required. The bench-
mark pipeline is able to generate its own datasets for evaluation.
Further, the raw data used for the paper’s results are included as
2https://github.com/cryptobern/tenderload
3https://github.com/cryptobern/tendergrid
4https://github.com/cryptobern/tendercounter

part of the artifact, if one wishes to e.g. only use the data analysis
part of the artifact on existing data.
A.3 Set Up
For detailed setup instructions, consult the main readme of the
tenderloadrepository.
A.3.1 Basic test.As a basic functionality test not involving large-
scale deployments, consider checking whether the deployment
pipeline works for a small network of e.g. 𝑛= 4VMs. Follow the
instructions in the main readme of the tenderload repository to
deploy the baseline version of CometBFT. Once the deployment
is through, check the log output of the CometBFT containers to
ensure that it is producing blocks.
At that point, consider performing a benchmark with e.g. invo-
cation rates between 10 and 100, and visualize the resulting data.
For this choice of parameters, expect to see a 1:1 relation between
invocation rate and throughput.
A.4 Evaluation Workflow
A.4.1 Major claims.
(C1): Adding support for asymmetric grid quorums to CometBFT
does not meaningfully impact its throughput, compared
to an equivalent benchmark for an unmodified version of
CometBFT, for LAN deployments with 𝑛= 28and 𝑛=
49machines. This is proven by experiments (E1) and (E2)
described in Sections 7 and 8 of our paper. Results of the
experiment are reported in Section 8, and visualized in
Figure 5 and Table 2.
A.4.2 Experiments.All instructions below, when referring to sec-
tions, refer to sections within the ‘Running the benchmark yourself’
Chapter of the mainREADME.mdin thetenderloadrepository.
(E1): [Baseline] [8 person-hours (mostly wait-time) + 4 compute-
weeks + 2 TiB disk]:
Preparation: Prepare a deployment of 𝑛= 28(respec-
tively 𝑛= 49) CometBFT instances using thebaselinever-
sion of CometBFT, by following Sections ‘Requirements’
through ‘Start CometBFT network’.
This should lead to a working deployment of CometBFT,
which produces blocks at a rate of one per second.
Execution: Run a benchmark by following Sections ‘Com-
piling and deploying the benchmark client’ and ‘Running
the benchmark client’.
After termination of the benchmark client, this should have
produced a set of raw benchmark data as a set of CSV and
JSON files on the host on which the client ran.
Results: Collect results and plot them by following Sec-
tions ‘Downloading benchmark results’ and ‘Plotting re-
sults’.
This should lead to a set of PNG images, containing invocation-
throughput plots.
(E2): [Grid] [10 person-hours (mostly wait-time) + 5 compute-
weeks + 2 TiB disk]:
Preparation: Equivalent toPreparationof (E1), but deploy
thegridversion of CometBFT instead. Be surenotto skip
the ‘Create sample asymmetric grid quorum system’ sub-
section.
Execution: Equivalent toExecutionof (E1). Be sure to read
and apply the instructions in the ‘Salvaging half-successful
benchmark runs’ Subsection.
Results:Equivalent toResultsof (E1).
A.5 Notes on Reusability
The benchmarking pipeline is flexible enough that parameters
such as the size of the system can be easily changed. This is doc-
umented in some detail within the tenderload repository, both
within readme files as well as with comments within the Ansible
scripts.
More generally, the deployment pipeline could be used to deploy
a fully-working CometBFT setup, including a replicated application
(so-called ‘ABCI app’) for purposes other than our benchmark.
Lastly, the asymmetric-quorums Go library could be used in ap-
plications operating with more advanced quorum structures — both
asymmetric as well as symmetric — than the traditional threshold
quorums.
